author: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate

slides.1: Adaptation is the half of climate action nobody puts on a poster. Yet here the rain disappears for months, and then one storm returns an entire year of it in two days.
slides.2: Everyone hears Climate Action and thinks of cutting carbon. Read the goal properly and half of it is about survival: drains that cope, homes that stand, and a supply that holds.
slides.3: We are officially a water-poor island, which sounds absurd in a place this wet. The mountains are simply too steep, so the rain reaches the sea long before it reaches a reservoir.
slides.4: Fewer typhoons sounds like good news until you remember that they refill our reservoirs. During the last great drought the storage simply ran out, rice fields cracked open, and the chip plants came close to stopping.
slides.5: Then the island floods. A single storm can deliver a year's rainfall in two days, and drains laid for a calmer century give up, turning shopping streets into brown rivers.
slides.6: Two questions follow, and neither has a comfortable answer. Can pipes designed for the last climate survive this one? And can we hold floodwater long enough to drink it in the dry season?
slides.7: Taiwan has not been standing still. The Forward-looking Water Grid has linked the pipelines of neighbouring cities, so when Kaohsiung runs short, spare supply can be pumped across from Tainan instead.
slides.8: Taipei and Taichung are being rebuilt as sponge cities. Solid concrete is giving way to pavement that lets rain through, and parks are sunk below the road so that a storm fills them first.
slides.9: Farming has changed as well. Computer-controlled drip irrigation gives a rice plant exactly the water it needs and nothing more, which saves millions of tons across the island every season.
slides.10: This is where STEM earns its place. Engineers have fitted sensors inside the mains, and the data they stream lets a computer locate a buried leak in minutes rather than months.
slides.11: We are also manufacturing water. Industrial wastewater is purified until it can go straight back into the production line, and plants on the coast can pull the salt out of seawater in an emergency.
slides.12: In the mountains the same thinking applies to landslides. Rather than pouring another concrete wall, engineers anchor the slope with rock and local planting, which keeps the mud out of our reservoirs.
slides.13: None of this is cheap, and the bill has to land somewhere. Recycling plants and deep pipelines cost billions of dollars, so the honest question is how we pay without squeezing ordinary households.
slides.14: There is a fairness problem hidden inside all of this. The wealthy technology cities receive the new systems first, while farming villages are the first to have their water cut during a drought.
slides.15: Other island nations face exactly these problems, and what we have learned could genuinely help them. Politics keeps Taiwan out of the major climate summits, so the knowledge has to travel by other routes.
slides.16: Finally, somebody has to check the work. A sponge park that nobody maintains is only landscaping, so citizens should be asking for the inspection data on our dams and drains every year.
slides.17: So where does that leave us? Sponge cities, a connected grid and a great deal of engineering are turning a vulnerable island into a prepared one. We cannot stop the storms, but we can meet them.
slides.18: Why should this matter to you? Because adaptation is still an unsolved design problem. Study earth science, coding or engineering, and meanwhile treat every drop you save at home as part of the answer.
slides.19: None of this should leave you feeling powerless. Human ingenuity and natural systems can work together rather than against each other, and Taiwan has both the skill and the nerve to prove it.
slides.20: The weather is not going to wait while we argue. So will you help build an island that can take the next storm? Taiwan can be ready to adapt, and that work starts today.
